title: Does Mayonnaise Need Refrigeration After Opening?

seo.title: Does Mayonnaise Need Refrigeration After Opening? Yes
seo.meta_description: Opened commercial mayonnaise should be refrigerated. USDA gives about two months as a refrigerated storage guide; homemade egg mayonnaise is more perishable.
seo.search_intent: Determine whether opened mayonnaise requires refrigeration, how long it keeps, and how homemade mayonnaise differs.

excerpt: Yes. Commercial mayonnaise should be refrigerated after opening. Its acidified formulation makes it more stable than homemade egg-and-oil mayonnaise, but once opened it belongs in the refrigerator; homemade mayo is even more perishable.
content_html:
Commercial mayonnaise should be refrigerated after opening. Industrial mayonnaise is acidified and made under controlled conditions, so it is more stable than a simple homemade emulsion of egg and oil. Opening the jar, however, introduces handling, air, and opportunities for contamination, and USDA storage guidance keeps opened mayonnaise cold.

As a practical reference, USDA and university extension guidance give about two months in the refrigerator for opened commercial mayonnaise. That is a storage guideline rather than a guarantee. The product label, actual refrigerator temperature, and handling still matter.

Commercial mayonnaise is not the same as raw egg mixed with oil

Commercial mayonnaise typically contains vinegar or another acid and is manufactured to a controlled formula. In the United States, the standard of identity specifies vegetable oil, acidifying ingredients, and egg-yolk-containing ingredients among its core components.

That acidity helps explain why a sealed commercial jar is far more stable than many people expect. It does not mean an opened jar should live in a pantry. Once the seal is broken, refrigeration protects both microbiological stability and the quality the manufacturer intended.

Homemade mayonnaise is a separate storage problem. If it contains raw or lightly treated egg, it does not have the same industrial controls or standardized acidity. It should be made in modest quantities, chilled promptly, and used much sooner.

Two months is a useful guide for opened commercial mayo

USDA recommends refrigerating commercial mayonnaise after opening and gives roughly two months as a storage window. University of Minnesota extension material provides the same general timeframe. Those estimates assume a refrigerator held at 40 °F/4 °C or below.

A jar does not magically become dangerous at midnight on day 61, and a manufacturer's label may provide a more specific instruction. The point of the guideline is to prevent an opened condiment from being forgotten for many months simply because it still smells acidic.

If mayonnaise moves slowly in your household, write the opening date on the lid. That simple habit is more reliable than guessing whether a jar was opened last week or last season.

Warm mayonnaise and mayonnaise-based dishes need different judgment

USDA emergency guidance says opened mayonnaise that has been above 50 °F/10 °C for more than eight hours should be discarded. The rule shows that the product's acidic formulation provides resilience but not unlimited room-temperature storage.

A finished dish can be more perishable than the mayonnaise itself. Potato salad, tuna salad, chicken salad, sandwiches, dips, and dressings may contain meat, fish, cooked vegetables, eggs, or dairy. The complete food should be managed according to its most perishable ingredients.

FoodSafety.gov's general rule is not to leave perishable food at room temperature for more than two hours, or one hour when the temperature is above 90 °F/32 °C. That is the better framework for picnic and buffet dishes.

Using mayonnaise in another dish also changes the storage question. A jar kept cold and handled with a clean utensil is one situation; potato salad, tuna salad, coleslaw, or a sandwich spread combines mayonnaise with other ingredients and may be exposed to room temperature during preparation and serving. The finished food should be judged by the most perishable components and by how long it has been warm, not by the acidity of commercial mayonnaise alone. That is why advice such as “mayonnaise is acidic, so the salad is safe” is too simplistic. Refrigerate the jar after opening, keep prepared dishes cold, and return leftovers promptly rather than using the condiment's shelf life as a shortcut for the entire recipe.

Clean handling matters, and obvious spoilage means discard

Use a clean utensil and avoid dipping a knife covered with tuna, cooked meat, egg, or crumbs back into the mayonnaise jar. Cross-contamination can introduce organisms and food residues that were never part of the controlled commercial formulation.

Minor oil separation can be a quality issue, but mold, gas, an abnormal odor, unusual discoloration, or a swollen container are reasons to discard the product. Do not taste suspicious mayonnaise as a safety test.

The practical rule is: opened commercial mayonnaise = refrigerate and use roughly within two months; homemade mayonnaise = shorter and more cautious storage; mayonnaise-based dishes = follow the storage needs of the whole dish. Acidification helps, but it does not make refrigeration optional after opening.

faq.question: How long does opened mayonnaise last in the refrigerator?
faq.answer: USDA and university extension guidance use about two months for properly refrigerated commercial mayonnaise.

faq.question: Can mayonnaise be left out overnight?
faq.answer: It is not good practice. USDA says opened mayonnaise held above 50 °F/10 °C for more than eight hours should be discarded, and mixed mayonnaise dishes can require much shorter limits.

faq.question: Does homemade mayonnaise last as long as commercial mayo?
faq.answer: No. Homemade mayonnaise lacks the same standardized acidification and processing and can be especially perishable when made with raw egg.
